title: Button switch
circuit: 3.3 V -> push button -> 220 ohm resistor -> red LED -> ground

expected.math: Button up: the path is broken, so no current flows (0 mA).

intro_lesson.title: Buttons are drawbridges
intro_lesson.idea: A button is like a drawbridge: down, cars cross; up, the road is broken. When you press the button, the bridge comes down and current can cross. When you let go, the bridge goes up and the current stops.
intro_lesson.question: What happens to the current when you let go of the button?
options: It stops, like cars at a raised bridge
intro_lesson.why: Letting go opens a gap in the path, so the current cannot get across.

mistakes.description: The button seems to be always on: current flows even when it is let go
mistakes.hint: You let go of the button, but current is still flowing. Something keeps the two sides of the button joined all the time. Look closely at how the button sits on the breadboard.
mistakes.explain: Current flows even when the button is up, so its two rows are joined some other way. A push button has pairs of legs that are always joined inside it. If the button is turned so that a joined pair reaches both rows, it is always on. Turn the button a quarter turn, so it joins the two rows only while it is pressed.

mini_lesson.title: A bridge that never goes up
mini_lesson.idea: A button is like a drawbridge that must go up to break the road. If its two sides are always joined, the bridge never goes up. Then current flows all the time, pressed or not.
mini_lesson.question: The LED stays on even when you let go of the button. What is most likely?
options: The two sides of the button are always joined
mini_lesson.why: If something always joins the two sides, the button can never break the path.

mistakes.description: The button does not join its two rows when it is pressed
mistakes.hint: You are holding the button, but no current flows, and nothing reaches the row after the button. The current is not getting across the button. Look at where the button's legs are.
mistakes.explain: When the button is pressed, its two rows should be joined, so the 3.3 volts reach the resistor. Here nothing reaches the row after the button. The button may be turned so that pressing it joins two legs in the same row, or a leg may not be pushed in. One side of the button should share a row with the red wire, and the other side a row with the resistor.

mini_lesson.title: A bridge that never comes down
mini_lesson.idea: A button is like a drawbridge: current can only cross when the bridge is down. If pressing does not join the two sides, the road stays broken. Then no current reaches the LED.
mini_lesson.question: You press the button, but the LED stays dark and no current flows. Why?
options: The button does not join its two sides
mini_lesson.why: If pressing does not join the two sides, there is still a gap, so no current flows.

mistakes.description: LED may be backwards, in the wrong row, or missing (the board cannot tell which)
mistakes.hint: You are holding the button and the full 3.3 volts reach the LED's row, but almost no current flows. So the current is stopped at the LED: it may be backwards, in the wrong row, or missing, and the board cannot tell which. Look at the LED's long leg, the one with the + in the drawing: see which row it is in, and which way it faces.
mistakes.explain: Three things can cause this, and the board cannot tell which one: the LED may be in backwards, it may be in the wrong row (its long leg not in the same row as the resistor), or it may be missing. The long leg (+) should share a row with the resistor, and the short leg (-) should lead to ground.

no_sensor.description: The resistor may be missing, or the LED may be backwards, in the wrong row, or missing (this board cannot measure current, so it cannot tell which)
no_sensor.hint: You are holding the button. First look at the LED. If it is very bright or feels warm, pull every wire out of the + line right now: the resistor may be missing. If the LED is dark, the current is stopped at the LED: it may be backwards, in the wrong row, or missing. Look at the LED's long leg, the one marked + in the drawing: which row is it in, and which way does it face?
no_sensor.explain: This board cannot measure current, so four things look the same to it. The 220 ohm resistor may be missing: then the LED gets far too much current and shines very brightly, so pull every wire out of the + line first. Or the LED may be in backwards, it may be in the wrong row (its long leg not in the same row as the resistor), or it may be missing: then it stays dark. The 220 ohm resistor must sit between the + side and the LED's long leg (+), and the short leg (-) should lead to ground.
no_sensor.screen: LED bright or warm?|Pull every wire|out of the + line!

mini_lesson.title: LEDs are one-way doors
mini_lesson.idea: An LED is like a one-way door. Current can only go through it in one direction, and only if the door is connected on both sides. If the door faces the wrong way or is not connected, the current stops.
mini_lesson.question: Current stops right at the LED. What could cause that?
options: The resistor is the wrong color
The LED faces the wrong way, or a leg is not connected
The power is too weak to light it
mini_lesson.why: An LED lets current through only one way, and only when both of its legs are connected.

mistakes.description: Circuit is not a closed loop: nothing reaches the LED's long leg while the button is held
mistakes.hint: You are holding the button, and the 3.3 volts get across it, but nothing is connected in the LED's row. Check that the resistor and the LED's long leg are both in the row you think they are in.
mistakes.explain: The circuit is not a closed loop. Each part must share a row with the next one: the button to the 220 ohm resistor, the resistor to the LED's long leg, and the LED's short leg to ground. The lit row is the LED's row, so make sure the resistor and the LED both reach it.

no_sensor.description: Circuit is not a closed loop (a part is in the wrong row), or the LED skips the resistor (this board cannot measure current, so it cannot tell which)
no_sensor.hint: You are holding the button. First look at the LED. If it is very bright or feels warm, pull every wire out of the + line right now: its long leg may skip the resistor. If it is dark, something is not connected: nothing reaches the LED's row. Check that each leg is in the row you think it is.
no_sensor.explain: The LED's row has nothing connected, and this board cannot measure current, so two things look the same to it. The LED's long leg may skip the 220 ohm resistor (for example, pushed into the row before it): then the LED gets far too much current and shines very brightly, so pull every wire out of the + line first. Or the circuit is not a closed loop: each part must share a row with the next one, the 220 ohm resistor to the LED's long leg, and the LED's short leg to ground. The lit row is the LED's row, so make sure the resistor and the LED both reach it.
no_sensor.screen: LED bright or warm?|Pull every wire|out of the + line!

mini_lesson.title: Circuits must be closed loops
mini_lesson.idea: Electric current only flows around a complete loop, from the power supply and back again. It is like a train track: if one piece is missing, the train cannot go around. A part in the wrong row is like a missing piece of track.
mini_lesson.question: What does current need in order to flow?
options: A complete loop with no gaps
mini_lesson.why: Current flows only around a closed loop, so one gap stops it everywhere.

mistakes.description: No resistor: the LED gets 3.3 V straight from the button
mistakes.hint: The current was far too high, so the power must stay off until it is fixed. What part in the circuit keeps the current small enough for the LED?
mistakes.explain: There was no resistor, so when the button was pressed the LED was connected straight to 3.3 volts. Nothing kept the current small, so it shot far past what the LED can handle, and that can burn it out. Put the 220 ohm resistor between the button and the LED's long leg.

mini_lesson.title: Resistors keep current small
mini_lesson.idea: A resistor slows down electric current, like a narrow pipe slows down water. Without one, a huge amount of current rushes through the LED. Too much current makes parts very hot and can burn them out.
mini_lesson.question: What is the job of the resistor in an LED circuit?
options: It makes the LED change color
It keeps the current small and safe
mini_lesson.why: The resistor limits the current, so the LED gets only as much as it can handle.
